LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST CONCEPTS · AGES 18–24 MONTHS

One — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the numbers with the only one that matters yet: one. Taught with a single finger, a single block, and single kisses, one becomes the number with a body and a meaning.

What is this?

One is the number word for a single thing — no crowd, no confusion. The card shows one object alone, and the finger you hold up is the number’s oldest, clearest picture.

What does it mean?

One is the number the rest of counting stands on: a toddler who owns one can feel two as one-and-another, and many as more than one. It is less a sum than a discovery — this much, and no more.

What does the child need to know?

Expect a finger held up — wobbly, or a fist with one knuckle escaping — and eventually a wan! spoken with it. The gesture is the number; the word rides along whenever it is ready.

Why this matters

One runs through daily life as the fair-share number: one biscuit, one book, one more kiss. A number attached to real hand-overs teaches itself at every transaction.

What it teaches

Number-word one, one-to-one handing, and the finger-symbol for one — the seed of all counting, planted with a single gesture.

Words to learn

onesinglefingeralonefirstmore

Say this to your child

“"One! Look — one finger. Just one. Here is one block for you… one! Can you show me one finger? There it is! One kiss… one more. One is just one, all by itself."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and hold up one finger beside it: one. Just the one finger — let the number be the whole show.
  2. Hand over one block, slowly, with the word: one block for you. Then wait. Then one more? — and hand a second: now there are two blocks. One makes others possible.
  3. Let your toddler try the finger: can you show me one? Any single finger raised — or attempted — is the number arriving.
  4. Hand out the real ones all week: one cracker, one sock, one kiss. Say one as each lands, one event per word.
  5. Read one in books too: one duck, one moon, one ball. The word travels light and lands everywhere.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows one object demonstrating the concept one for toddlers — a single thing, alone in the picture. Ask your toddler to hold up one finger next to it, one finger only.

Ask your child

"Can you show me one finger?" "How many blocks?" "Is that one or lots?" "Can I have one kiss?"

What your child can say or do

A raised index finger is the classic answer, complete with wobble. Wan! or duh! (for one) arrives with practice; the gesture leads the word by weeks, exactly as it should.

Out in the real world

Ones are handed over all day: one banana, one shoe, one hug at the gate. Attach the word at the moment of hand-over and the number keeps honest company.

Try it together

One-at-a-time post: your toddler posts one block into the box, receives it back, posts it again — one! each round. Single-file handing is the game, and one gets said until it is worn in.

Understanding check

Ask for one finger from across the room. A single finger — even a thumb, even attempted — passes. Then hand over two blocks and ask which is one: a pause before taking means the number is being counted, not just heard.

Parent tips

One event, one word: say one as each single thing lands and stay silent between landings — the gaps are what make one mean single. Do not rush two; one has a whole year of work ahead and plenty of everyday jobs.

Staying safe

No safety angle here — this is a sitting, handing, finger game. The only note: the objects being counted one by one stay bigger than a toilet-roll tube, as everything does at this age.

This lesson pairs with the One flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Concepts (Toddler 2).
